outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version that preserves the imagery, voice, and meaning while refining the language for greater eloquence:

---

That day in December, I sat down beside Miss Muffet of Montgomery. I was weary beyond measure—my feet swollen from stitching seams on filthy fabric, my body aching from pedaling the rusty Singer, the dingy cotton thread forever snagging in the needle's eye. All my life long I had glided through endless reams, loathsome with tears, dreaming of my own silken self.

It was not as they all tell it. Miss Liberty Muffet did not startle at the sight of me—not exactly. They dragged me away: a thousand kicking legs pinned down. Yet the rest of me, I tell you, was a cloud—beautiful trouble upon the dead December horizon, come to sit in judgment. How many miles, as the Jim Crow flies? Over oceans, and then some.

I rumbled. They could not hold me down—not for long. No. My feet were tired. My eyes were sore. My heart was raw from hemming the soiled edges of Miss L. Muffet's garment.

So I rode again—a thousand bloody miles, as the Crow flies—that day in December, long remembered, when I sat down beside Miss Muffet of Montgomery. I said, as the old joke goes: What's in the bowl, Thief? I said: That is your curse. I said: This is my way.

She slipped from her frock, disembarked, and settled in the suburbs—deaf, mute, lewd, and blind. The bowl she left behind. The empty bowl is mine. The spoiled dress, mine. Jim Crow dies, and the ravens come bearing crumbs. They say: Eat, and be satisfied. But I fast, and pray, and ride.

---

A note: this piece derives much of its force from its deliberate dialect and fractured, incantatory rhythm (for example, "Feets swole," "a pedalin'"). My revision smooths these toward standard, "professional" prose, but in doing so it inevitably softens some of the original's raw poetic voice. If you'd prefer, I can offer a lighter polish that retains more of the original's distinctive cadence and vernacular power.
outputs.L2: On that December day, I took a seat beside Miss Muffet of Montgomery. Countless exhaustions weighed on me. My feet had swollen from stitching seams across grimy cloth; I ached from working the pedal of that corroded Singer; grubby cotton thread had clogged the needle's eye. Throughout my whole existence I'd fed endless yards through the machine, all of them hateful with weeping. Yet I dreamed of my own silken form. The story didn't unfold the way everyone claims. Miss Liberty Muffet didn't recoil when she saw me—not precisely. They dragged me off, my thousand thrashing legs held fast. But the remainder of me, I promise you, was a cloud. Gorgeous mischief hanging on the lifeless December sky. Arriving to render my verdict. How far is it as the Jim Crow travels? Across seas and then farther still. I let out a rumble. They couldn't keep me pinned. For long. No. My feet had worn out. My eyes ached. My heart was scraped raw from finishing the soiled hems of Miss L. Muffet's clothing. So I traveled once more. A thousand bloodstained miles trailing the Crow on that December day I'll never forget, the day I settled down next to Miss Muffet of Montgomery. I asked—as the old joke goes—What's sitting in the bowl, Thief? I told her—That is your curse. I told her—This is my path. She peeled off her dress, stepped down, moved out to the suburbs, hearing nothing, saying nothing, indecent, sightless. The bowl stayed behind. That empty bowl belongs to me now. The ruined gown too. Jim Crow perishes and ravens arrive bearing crumbs. They tell me—Eat until you're full. But I go hungry, I pray, and I ride onward.
outputs.L3:
# The Seamstress's Reckoning

I am worn to the bone, a seamstress spent by labor that never ceases. My feet are swollen from standing hour upon hour; my eyes ache from squinting at seams in dim light; and my heart is rubbed raw from the endless work of sewing garments I will never wear—fine clothes stitched for another's shoulders while my own hands remain empty. This is the life pressed upon me, a life of relentless toil in service to those who neither see nor value me.

But let me tell you a different kind of nursery rhyme. You know the story of Little Miss Muffet, who sat upon her tuffet, content and undisturbed. I reimagine her now as Miss Muffet of Montgomery—a symbol of the whole edifice of Jim Crow, of Southern privilege built upon my exhaustion. And so I sat down beside her. That simple act, that quiet claiming of space, became my declaration.

They removed me, of course. Hands seized me and cast me out, as they had done to so many before. But understand this: though I was forced from my seat, I refused to be held down for good. My sitting was not idleness—it was judgment rendered. My presence was a verdict passed upon a system that thought itself eternal. Cast out, I rose again; pushed down, I returned. My resistance was not a single moment but an enduring posture, a refusal repeated until refusal itself became my strength.

In time, Miss Muffet could not bear my nearness. She abandoned everything she had guarded so jealously—her privileged garment, her precious bowl—and fled into the suburbs, retreating behind new walls, making herself "deaf, mute, lewd, and blind." She would not hear, would not speak, would not see what she had wrought. She left me there with the empty bowl and the spoiled dress: the hollow remains of a privilege that had curdled, the ruined inheritance of her flight.

And so Jim Crow lay dying at last. In his final hours, he offered me crumbs—small tokens of false satisfaction, meant to quiet me, to make me grateful for scraps. But I would not take them. I turned away from that meager comfort. Instead I chose to fast and to pray, to hunger deliberately rather than be fed on lies. My journey was not finished, and it would not end in gratitude for crumbs. Defiant still, I rose and walked on.
outputs.L4:
# The Tuffet Revisited

I've spent my days on curds and whey,
threading needles, cloth to cloth,
my fingers raw, my back a knot,
while Miss Muffet takes her seat
upon the tuffet built for her—
that cushioned throne I stitched myself,
the very velvet, the very thread,
these hands that ache have laid for years.

They tell me spiders came and sat.
They tell me she was frightened off.
But I have known the crawling thing,
the dark shape settling at my side—
it never scared *me* from my place.
No, I have carried it all day,
that eight-legged weight of *know your row,
your seat, your fountain, and your door.*

Tonight my feet have simply stopped.
The bus is full. The driver waits.
He says the word he always says,
the word that moves me toward the back
like furniture, like folded coats,
like something bought and paid and owned.

But I am tired in my bones—
not sleepy-tired, no, deeper down,
the tired of a hundred years,
of *yes sir, no sir, right away,*
of stitching thrones I cannot climb.

So here. I sit. I take the bowl
that Muffet left when she ran off,
this bowl of curds gone thin and gray,
this seat still warm from her white weight.
I claim it now. I set it down.
I fold my hands upon my lap.

It is not much. I know the cost.
The spider watches. It won't leave.
The tuffet's mine for just tonight,
and men with clubs will come to say
the bowl was never mine to hold.

But something's shifted in the room.
The rhyme is broken. I remain.
Let Muffet run. Let spiders spin.
I've eaten of the curds and whey.
I've kept my seat. I've said my word.

And though the morning brings the fight,
the courts, the cells, the crawling dread,
the aching years still stretched ahead—
tonight the tuffet holds my name,
tonight I did not walk away.
outputs.L5:
**That December to Miss**

That December was unlike any other. The snow fell softly over the quiet town, blanketing the streets in a silence that felt almost sacred. I remember thinking that no season could ever capture such a perfect stillness again.

It was during that December that I first met Miss Caldwell. She was the new teacher at our small school, and everyone whispered about how different she seemed from the others. She carried herself with a warmth that melted the cold walls of our classroom. That kindness was something none of us would ever forget.

Miss Caldwell had a way of making even the dullest lessons feel like adventures. She would tell stories that transported us far beyond the frosted windows, into worlds we never knew existed. Every child adored her, and I suppose that is why her departure hurt so deeply.

By the end of that December, we learned she would be moving away. The news struck us hard. It's strange how much you can miss someone who was only in your life for a short while. We would miss her laughter, her patience, and the gentle encouragement she offered whenever we stumbled.

On her last day, she gave each of us a small handwritten note. Mine simply said, "Never stop dreaming." That message stayed with me for years, a reminder that some people leave marks on our hearts that no amount of time can erase.

Now, whenever December arrives and the first snowflakes begin to fall, I think of Miss Caldwell. I remember that unforgettable winter, and I understand that some memories are meant to last forever.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental prose poem that reimagines Rosa Parks and the Montgomery bus boycott through the nursery rhyme "Little Miss Muffet," blending civil rights history with the imagery of spiders, thread, and Jim Crow.
counterfactuals.output:
# Little Miss Muffet Refuses

*after Montgomery, after the thread that would not break*

---

She sat. Not on a tuffet but the fourth row back, where the ordinance
said her body belonged, where the whey of segregation curdled
in December air. Little Miss Muffet, they might have called her,
diminishing—as if her spine were a footnote, as if her *no*
were merely a child's rhyme, a thing to be recited and forgotten.

*Along came a spider.*

Jim Crow spun in eight directions: WHITE ONLY, COLORED WATER,
the arachnid architecture of a South stitched shut. See how
the web glistens, how it catches light like justice, how it catches
*everything* and lets nothing pass. The spider does not hurry.
The spider has all the time that law can give it.

But listen—

There is another thread. Older. It runs from Rosa's stillness
through the seamstress hands that knew the weight of cloth,
that measured hems and understood how one loose stitch
unravels the whole garment of a lie.

*Who sat down beside her?*

Not the spider. *Her.* Forty thousand feet that would not ride.
The boycott braided itself: each walking woman a filament,
each shoe-sole a small refusal, and the web that meant to trap her
became the very net that caught a city, held it, would not
*let it go* until the wheels of profit whined and buckled.

She did not run away.

That is the revision. That is the crack in the nursery's spine.
Muffet stayed. Muffet folded her hands like a woman
folds fresh linen, and the spider—all its geometry, its patient
poison, its *how-things-have-always-been*—found her curds
untouched, her whey intact, her body a stubborn punctuation
the sentence could not swallow.

---

*Along came a spider. And she watched it drown*
*in a sea of walking. In three hundred and eighty-one*
*days of soles on pavement. In the thread that would not break*
*because it was never thread at all—*

it was *nerve.*
it was *no.*
it was a woman
who unspun December
into spring.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a surreal, stream-of-consciousness monologue from the perspective of a Black seamstress who becomes a spider, weaving together themes of labor, segregation, and defiance in December.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Weaving

December, and my fingers know the cold before the rest of me does. Been sewing since the light was still deciding whether to come up over the Woolworth's, since before the buses started their groaning down Jefferson with all those faces pressed to glass, colored faces in the back, always the back, and me here at the machine, needle going down-up-down like a heartbeat that don't belong to me anymore.

They pay me by the piece. Did I tell you that? By the piece, like I'm pieces myself, like you could lay me out on a pattern and cut along the dotted—

—and now there's more of my fingers than there used to be.

*Count them.*

Eight. No, that's not—when did I—

The spinnerets come quiet. That's the thing nobody tells you about becoming. You expect thunder. You expect the burning bush. But it comes quiet as a thread pulled through, quiet as the way they built the whole city so a woman like me learns to enter through the alley, through the back, through the *understood.* My body just kept doing what my body was made to do. Make the thread. Make the cloth. Make the beautiful thing you'll never wear me to.

I climb the wall now.

The wall between the water fountains, I climb it. The wall of the fitting room where the sign says who and who-not, I climb it. Spin my silk across the "WHITES ONLY" until the letters go soft behind the gauze of me, until you can't read the meanness for the lace. *Look what I made of your rules. Look what I stitched across your borders.*

December wind through the loading dock and I am eight-legged and patient. Patience is a thing they think they taught me. Sit still, gal. Wait your turn, gal. Be grateful for the piecework, gal. But they didn't teach me patience—my grandmother did, threading a needle by lamplight, and *her* grandmother did, and the patience was never for them. The patience was the long game. The patience was the web taking shape while the fly still thinks he owns the room.

I weave the names in. All the names. The ones from the fields into the ones from the factory into the ones I'll never know. My silk remembers what the ledgers tried to forget. Every unpaid hour spins out silver. Every *no* becomes an anchor-line. And the whole trembling architecture of it holds—holds!—because a web that gives is a web that does not break.

They'll come with the broom in the morning.

They always come with the broom.

But brooms are for the weak-woven, and honey, I have been practicing my whole life. Sweep me down and I climb the corner. Climb me out and I'm already in the eaves, in the ductwork, in the walls of the house you built on the backs of the backs of the backs of us. I am in the seams of your Sunday suit. I am the thread you cannot find to pull.

December. The cold knows my name and speaks it gentle.

Let me tell you what defiance is. Defiance is not the fist, though I love the fist. Defiance is the *staying.* Defiance is spinning through the frost when your body screams to fold. Defiance is making beauty from the very silk they wrung out of your suffering and hanging it where the sun will catch it come morning—

—so that even the men with the brooms

have to stop.

Have to look.

Have to see the thing I made

before they try, and fail,

to sweep me

away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a dense, allusive poem that mashes up "Little Miss Muffet" with the phrase "as the crow flies" and the story of a tired woman who refuses to give up her seat.
counterfactuals.output:
**Tuffet, Montgomery Line**

She sat upon her tuffet—no, her seat,
the whey of morning curdling in her chest,
a weariness that measures, as the crow
flies, the ledger-miles from field to feet.

But Jim, that crow, came down beside her, spread
his oil-black wing across the aisle's meridian,
and bid her rise, go frighten to the back
where spiders spin their separate-but-equal thread.

She would not. Note the arachnid architecture:
how threads pull straight, how every tuffet's queen
is told to scatter—*shoo, girl, mind your curds*—
yet December stiffened her to statuary posture.

The rhyme demanded flight. She stayed. The bus
became a nursery gutted of its lesson,
and forty-two thousand feet walked out the meter
of that refusal, singing, *none of us,*

*not one, will rise.* So measure it: the crow
still thinks in straight lines, thinks a wing outruns
a woman rooted spider-proof and plain—
but grief walks crooked, and the long way's slow,

and slow is how the tuffet turns to throne.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a piece of literary flash fiction or prose poetry that uses fractured, lyrical language to explore Rosa Parks, Miss Muffet, tuffets, curds and whey, and the crushing weight of Jim Crow laws.
counterfactuals.output:
# On the Matter of Seats

*

There was a woman who sat down.

There was a woman who would not stand.

*

Little Miss Muffet sat on her tuffet—that small hill, that grassy throne, that *permission* to occupy space—and no one told her the earth beneath her was zoned. No sign said WHITE ONLY on the tuffet. The curds came sweet. The whey came cool. She ate what was hers because it was hers because *she* was hers.

*

Consider the tuffet: a place to rest. A birthright of the bone-tired body. How the nursery gave it freely to the golden child and how the ordinance took it, seat by seat, from the woman whose feet had walked ten thousand miles of *yes ma'am* and *no sir* and *right away.*

*

Rosa. Say it like a bloom. Say it like a wound.

*

She sat on the tuffet of a Montgomery bus and the spider came—not black, not spinning, but *legislated*—came down beside her in the shape of a man's demand, in the shape of *move,* in the shape of the whole state's crushing architecture bearing down on one woman's spine, on the last inch of her patience worn to lace.

*

But here the rhyme *breaks.*

*

For Miss Muffet, frightened, ran.
And Rosa—

Rosa did not run.

*

The curds soured in the heat of the century. The whey went bitter as the back of the bus, as the balcony seat, as the water that tasted the same but was poured through the fountain of *lesser.* Jim Crow, that scarecrow king, that patchwork tyrant stitched from ledgers and lynch-rope and law—he wanted every daughter *afraid of the spider.* He wanted every daughter *gone from the tuffet.*

*

Weight. Speak of the weight.

The weight of a look that says *you are less.*
The weight of a law that agrees.
The weight of the seat you paid for and cannot keep.
The weight, the weight, the whole gray steeple of a nation's *no* pressed down upon the small cathedral of a body that only wanted—

*

*—to sit.*

*

And so she stayed. And staying, *rose.*

Do you hear the trick the language plays? To *stay* is to *rise.* The stillest woman on the bus became the movement. The tuffet became the fault line. The curds and whey of a child's small hunger became the milk of a nation's overdue reckoning, spilled at last, spreading white and undeniable across the courthouse floor.

*

Here is the ending they don't put in the rhyme:

The spider did not win.

The frightened girl grew tired of running and turned, mid-flight, and *sat back down.*

And the whole world, watching, learned the weight a single seat can hold.

*

There was a woman who sat down.

There was a woman who would not stand.

They were the same woman.

She is sitting there still.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an avant-garde retelling of the Montgomery bus protest narrated by an insect-woman, full of wordplay ("Jim Crow flies," "myriad-weary," "silk-self"), ending with ravens, fasting, and an empty bowl.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Molt of Montgomery

*(as sung by the mantis-mother, she of the sixfold ache)*

---

I am the insect-woman, myriad-weary, and I remember the year the whole city learned to *walk*.

Listen with your antennae. I speak in the register of the small.

---

There was a bus, and the bus was a beetle of steel, and it crawled the boulevard swallowing us into its abdomen. Front-thorax for some. Hind-gut for others. *Jim Crow flies*—oh, how he flew, that carrion king, that fly of feathered spite, laying his eggs of *No* in every open mouth. He buzzed the ordinance. He droned the ordinal: *first, first, first,* he said, and *last, last, last,* to us.

But a seamstress sat. A *silk-self* woman, spinner of her own refusal, she anchored her thread to the seat and would not be re-spooled. *Rosa,* they named her, though I knew her by her stillness—the stillness of a chrysalis that has decided.

*Move,* said the driver-drone.

*I have moved enough,* said the silk-self. *I have moved my whole life-length and arrived nowhere.*

And the thread held.

---

O the *arrest*, the arrest, which is only a rest with an *a* of anger fastened to its front. They caged her. They thought a cage could hold a woman who had already made herself a cocoon.

Foolish. You cannot arrest a metamorphosis. You can only *witness* it.

---

Then—the swarm.

We did not fly. That was the wonder of it. We, the winged, chose the *foot*. Forty thousand *foot-souls*, myriad-weary, myriad-willing, we grounded our gossamer and pressed our tarsi to the pavement. We walked the *boycott*—that lovely blunt word, *boy-cot*, the child's bed empty, the seat unwarmed, the fare unpaid.

*Let the beetle starve,* we hummed. *Let the steel abdomen hollow.*

Three-hundred-eighty-one days. I counted them on my segmented belly. Each dawn a new *instar*. Each mile a shed skin. We left our old selves in husks along the roadside—glittering, discarded, *free*.

The rain came. We walked.
The heat came. We walked.
The threats came, hissing like wasps at the hive-door. We walked.

A preacher-moth rose among us, drawn to the terrible lamp of the moment, and he did not burn. He *fanned* it. *Love your enemy,* he said, and the strangeness of it broke us open like ripe pods. *Meet hate with the soft underwing.*

---

And the beetle *did* starve.

Its coffers grew light as an emptied exoskeleton. The city's cruel machinery, un-fed, began to *molt* against its will. High up in some marble comb, the black-robed elders read the law and found it *lousy*—infested, at last, with justice's slow maggots. *Unequal,* they ruled. *Unconstitutional.* The words fell like the wings off a dead thing.

Jim Crow flies buzzed once, twice—

then dropped.

---

Now hear the ending, small ones, for every metamorphosis owes a debt to the dark.

The ravens came.

Not carrion-ravens. *Wisdom-ravens*, ink-feathered, the ones who fed the fasting prophets in the old dry stories. They settled on the wires above the resting buses. They watched us with their coin-bright eyes.

And I—the insect-woman, the mantis-mother, she of the sixfold ache—I set down my bowl.

The bowl was empty.

Understand: the empty bowl is not the bowl of defeat. It is the bowl of the *faster*, who has given up the small hunger to feed the enormous one. It is the bowl of the boycott, unfilled by fare. It is the bowl of the chrysalis, who eats nothing and becomes everything. It is the belly of the starved beetle, hollowed into surrender.

*Empty,* the ravens croaked. *Empty is how the new thing enters.*

I folded my six weary limbs. I fasted from despair. I held the empty bowl up to the emptied bus, to the emptied law, to the emptied throne of the fly-king—

and into that emptiness, at last,

something like morning

was *poured*.

---

*This is the molt of Montgomery.*
*Walk it into your children.*
*Keep the bowl empty. Keep the thread taut.*
*Keep the strange soft wing outstretched.*

The ravens are still watching.

They are waiting to be fed by our fasting again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
